claims.text: Rapid, transient heating synchronizes nucleation across all noble-metal precursors.
Synchronized nucleation is the key mechanistic driver for forming homogeneous noble metal–based high-entropy alloy nanoparticles.
Slower heating permits differential nucleation and elemental diffusion.
Differential nucleation and elemental diffusion under slower heating lead to phase separation and heterogeneous structures.
The proposed starting material is a homogeneously mixed, unreduced multimetal precursor containing noble-metal ions or complexes, often with similar ligand environments.
Rapid thermal shock should be compared with slower heating while all other synthesis parameters are held constant.
Heating on a millisecond-to-second timescale induces nearly simultaneous nucleation under inert or reducing conditions.
A brief, intense thermal pulse causes simultaneous reduction and nucleation of all metal species.
Simultaneous reduction and nucleation minimize elemental segregation and enable full nanoscale solid-solution alloying.
A high transient temperature minimizes differences among the nucleation activation energies of individual noble metals.
Rapid quenching locks in a homogeneous alloy structure.
Rapid quenching preserves high surface-atom exposure needed for catalysis.
Rapid transient heating will produce single-phase HEA nanoparticles.
Rapid transient heating will produce a uniform elemental distribution in the nanoparticles.
Rapid transient heating will yield greater noble-metal surface exposure than slower heating.
Slower heating will produce phase-separated domains, elemental segregation, and uncontrolled morphology.
The mechanism generally applies when differences in metal reduction or nucleation energies are moderate and the system contains approximately five to seven elements.
Strongly dissimilar metal chemistry can cause the proposed rapid-heating mechanism to fail.
Precursor ligands, ligand stripping, solvents, and stabilizers can alter metal-species kinetics enough to dominate nanoparticle formation.
A failure of transient heating to produce significantly greater homogeneity, single-phase character, and noble-metal surface exposure than the slower-heating control would falsify the hypothesis.
